gitignore.short: A file listing names and folders, such as keys and large raw data, that git add skips while they are untracked; it does not remove files already committed.

absolute-reference.short: A spreadsheet address with $ signs, such as $E$1, that stays the same when a formula is copied to other cells.

afue.short: The share of a furnace's fuel energy that ends up as heat in the home over a heating season, under a standard test.

aggregator.short: A company that enrols many customers' devices, offers their combined response to a grid operator or utility, and shares the payment with the owners.

annuity-factor.short: What one dollar paid every year for a number of years is worth today, once each dollar is discounted.

api-key.short: A private code that identifies you to an online data service; treat it like a password and keep it out of shared files.

array.short: An ordered list or table of numbers; a linear program's costs c, rule table A and limits b are arrays.

assert.short: A line of code that stops a program with a message when a stated condition is false.

attributed-emissions.short: The share of a grid's CO₂ assigned to one user, for example each MWh it uses times that hour's average emission factor.

agc.short: The grid operator's computer system that raises or lowers plants over minutes to bring frequency back to 60 Hz.

average-emission-factor.short: An hour's CO₂ from all the plants that ran, divided by all the electricity used in that hour.

average-power.short: The energy used over a period divided by the length of that period.

balancing.short: Keeping the power that plants make equal to the power that people use, at every moment.

balancing-authority.short: The organisation that keeps supply and demand balanced, moment to moment, in its own part of the grid.

balancing-loop.short: A feedback loop with an odd number of negative links, which tends to oppose the change that started it; with long delays it can overshoot or swing back and forth.

baseline.short: An estimate of what a customer would have used without a demand-response event, against which the cut is measured.

basis-risk.short: The risk that the price where a plant sells differs from the price at which its contract settles, such as its node against a trading hub.

battery-duration.short: How many hours a battery can discharge at its rated power: its energy in MWh divided by its power in MW.

battery-margin.short: What a battery earns per megawatt-hour it discharges, after paying for the power it charged and the energy lost on the way.

benchmark.short: A case whose right answer is known in advance, from a hand calculation or an independent source, used to test a model.

forecast-bias.short: The average signed miss of a forecast, showing whether it tends to run too high or too low.

binding-constraint.short: A rule that holds exactly at the selected plan, with no room to spare; loosening it may or may not improve the best cost.

boolean-operators.short: AND, OR and NOT, the words that join search terms: AND narrows a search, OR widens it, NOT leaves terms out.

branch.short: A movable label on a line of commits, so a what-if can grow without changing the main line of work.

branch-and-bound.short: A search for the best whole-number plan that solves relaxations, splits on a fractional decision (off or on), and drops every branch whose bound cannot beat the best plan found.

break-even-price.short: The sale price at which a project's net present value is exactly zero; when electricity is its only revenue, with the same costs, output and discounting, it equals the plant's levelized cost.

bridge-power.short: Temporary on-site generation that serves part of a load until its grid connection is ready.

buffer.short: The zone within a set distance of a map feature, such as everything within 1 km of a wind turbine.

building-code.short: The rules a city, county or state sets for how new buildings must be built, such as insulation, wiring and safety.

bus.short: A point of the network where plants, loads and lines meet, such as a substation; a network model has one balance rule per bus.

caidi.short: Customer Average Interruption Duration Index: the average minutes to restore one interruption, SAIDI divided by SAIFI.

capacity.short: The most power a plant can produce at once, often called its nameplate size.

capacity-credit.short: The share of a plant's size that planners count on to meet the year's peak, judged by how much it lowers the risk of a shortage.

capacity-expansion.short: An optimization model that decides what to build, as well as how to run it, at least cost.

capacity-factor.short: The energy a plant actually made over a period, divided by the energy it would have made running at full capacity the whole time.

capital-cost.short: The money spent to build a power plant, usually given per kilowatt of capacity, before it makes any electricity.

capital-recovery-factor.short: The share of a building cost that must be repaid each year, with interest, to pay it off over a given number of years.

capture-ratio.short: The average price a plant earns per megawatt-hour it produces, divided by the average market price across all hours: hours with more output count more.

carbon-budget.short: A cap on the total CO₂ emitted over many years, a limit on a stock rather than on one year's flow.

carbon-intensity.short: The CO2 emitted for each unit of electricity, for example in tonnes per megawatt-hour.

carbon-price.short: A charge per tonne of CO2 emitted, added to costs so that cleaner choices become relatively cheaper.

carnot-limit.short: The largest share of heat any heat engine can turn into work: 1 minus the cold temperature over the hot temperature, both in kelvin.

carrying-cost.short: What money tied up in buildings or equipment costs while they earn nothing: the interest, or the return it could have earned elsewhere.

causal-loop-diagram.short: A map of causes and effects in which every arrow carries a sign: plus if more of the cause brings more of the effect, minus if it brings less.

chain-reaction.short: A run of fissions in which the neutrons from each split go on to split more atoms; a reactor holds it steady, each generation as large as the last.

chance-constraint.short: A rule required to hold with a chosen probability, for example at least a 95% chance of meeting a week's demand, rather than with certainty.

checksum.short: A short fingerprint computed from a file's bytes, such as SHA-256, that changes if even one byte of the file changes.

circuit-breaker.short: A switch that opens by itself when it senses a fault, cutting the power to everything beyond it, and can be closed again.

clearing-price.short: The price at which supply meets demand in a market, paid to every seller that runs in that hour.

clone.short: A complete new copy of a repository, with its files and its whole history.

clustering.short: Grouping similar items, such as days with similar demand and weather, so that one representative can stand for each group.

co-op.short: An electric utility owned by the members it serves, common in rural areas.

coefficient-of-performance.short: Heat a heat pump delivers divided by the electricity it uses; a COP of 3 means 3 kWh of heat for each kWh of electricity.

combined-cycle.short: A gas power plant that burns gas in a turbine and uses the hot exhaust to make steam for a second turbine, so it gets more electricity from the same fuel.

commit.short: A recorded snapshot of a project's tracked files as they were staged, with a message, its author and time, and a link to the commit before it.

concentrated-solar.short: Mirrors focus sunlight to heat a fluid; the heat runs a turbine or a process, and it can be stored for hours in tanks.

concept-matrix.short: A table with papers in rows and ideas in columns, coded by a stated rule, that shows what a literature covers and what it leaves out.

condenser.short: The part of a steam plant that cools the used steam back into water, so it can be pumped back to the boiler; most of the plant's waste heat leaves here.

conditional-price.short: A price read from a linear program in which the on/off decisions are held fixed; it holds only for that commitment.

conflict-of-interest.short: A financial or other tie that could bias, or seem to bias, a researcher's work, and so must be declared.

congestion.short: A power line carrying all it is allowed to, so cheaper power cannot reach where it is needed and prices can differ by location.

congestion-rent.short: What loads pay at their locational prices minus what generators are paid at theirs; in a DC model it equals the sum, over the full lines, of each line's shadow price times its flow.

constraint.short: A rule every solution must obey, such as supply equals demand or no plant above its size.

control-rod.short: A rod of neutron-absorbing material that is pushed into a reactor core to slow the chain reaction, or pulled out to speed it up.

coolant.short: The fluid, such as water, helium, liquid sodium or molten salt, that carries heat away from a reactor core.

coordinate-reference-system.short: The rule that ties map coordinates to places on Earth; some keep areas true, others keep distances, none keeps both everywhere.

utc.short: The world reference clock, with no daylight saving; EIA stamps its hourly grid data in it.

coordination-cost.short: What it costs to enrol, meter, control and pay each device or customer in a program, whatever the device's size.

cost-of-capital.short: The yearly return an owner's lenders and investors require on money tied up in equipment; the real cost of capital leaves inflation out.

cost-of-service.short: What it costs a utility to serve a customer or a class of customers: energy, plants, wires, meters and billing.

counterfactual.short: What would have happened without the change being judged; every saving or effect is measured against one.

credit-roles.short: A standard list of 14 names for what each author did, such as conceptualization (shaping the question), data curation (cleaning and documenting data) and formal analysis.

criticality.short: The steady state of a chain reaction, with a multiplication factor of exactly 1; it is a reactor's normal operating state, not an emergency.

critical-load.short: The loads that must stay on in an outage, such as a hospital or a water plant; the rest can be switched off.

cross-subsidy.short: When some customers pay more than the cost of serving them so that others can pay less.

cube-law.short: The power carried by the wind grows with the cube of its speed (twice the speed, eight times the power); a turbine's output follows it only between its cut-in and rated speeds.

curtailment.short: Turning a wind or solar farm below what the weather allows, usually because the grid has more power than it can use at that moment.

customer-class.short: A group of customers, such as homes or businesses, that a utility bills under the same tariffs.

customer-hours.short: Customers without power times the hours they are out: 100 customers out for 3 hours is 300 customer-hours.

customer-minutes.short: The number of customers without power times the minutes they wait: 10 homes dark for an hour is 600 customer-minutes.

cut-in-speed.short: The lowest wind speed at which a turbine starts to make electricity.

cut-out-speed.short: The wind speed above which a turbine shuts down to protect itself.

data-licence.short: The terms under which a dataset may be used and shared, such as public domain, CC BY or a signed data agreement.

data-note.short: A short record of where a dataset came from, its licence, units and time base, and every cleaning step with its rule, count and effect.

dataframe.short: A pandas table with named columns and an index, such as one row per hour.

day-ahead-forecast.short: A grid operator's estimate, made the day before, of how much power customers will use in each hour.

daylight-saving-time.short: Clocks moved an hour ahead in summer, giving one 23-hour day in spring and one 25-hour day in autumn.

dc-power-flow.short: A linear approximation of real-power flows that sets each line's flow from the voltage-angle difference across it, holds voltage magnitudes fixed, assumes small angles, and leaves out losses and reactive power.

decay-heat.short: Heat that the radioactive fission products in used fuel keep giving off after the chain reaction has stopped.

decision-analysis.short: A structured way to choose among options under uncertainty, weighing each possible outcome by how likely and how valuable it is.

decision-variable.short: A quantity the model is free to choose, such as how much each plant makes each hour.

demand.short: The total power that all users on a grid draw at a given moment.

demand-charge.short: A part of a power bill charged per kW of the customer's busiest hour (or interval) in the month, not per kWh.

demand-response.short: Electricity users cutting or shifting their use when the grid asks, usually in return for a payment.

deterministic-equivalent.short: A chance constraint rewritten as an ordinary rule with a safety margin, for example planning for the demand level that is exceeded with only the allowed probability.

developer.short: The company that plans, builds and owns a new facility, such as a factory or a data center.

diff.short: A line-by-line list of what changed between two versions of a file, with removed lines marked minus and added lines plus.

difference-in-differences.short: A comparison of how much an outcome changed in a group that got a programme against how much it changed in a similar group that did not.

discount-rate.short: The yearly rate used to turn money paid or received in the future into its value today.

dispatch.short: Deciding how much power each plant should make, hour by hour or minute by minute.

dispatchable.short: A power plant whose output the operator can turn up or down on request, such as a gas plant.

distribution.short: The lower-voltage part of the grid, from substations along feeders and laterals to homes and businesses.

dominated-plan.short: A plan that another plan beats on every count: no more cost, no more emissions, and better on at least one.

dot-product.short: The sum of the products of two vectors' matching entries, such as costs times outputs, added up.

duck-curve.short: The daily shape of demand minus solar output, with a dip at midday and a steep climb in the evening.

duration-curve.short: A year of hourly values sorted from highest to lowest, showing for how many hours each level is reached.

econometrics.short: Statistics applied to economic data, often to estimate whether a change caused an effect.

efficiency.short: The share of the energy put into a plant or device that comes out in the useful form, such as electricity.

electric-current.short: The flow of electric charge through a wire, measured in amperes (A); for the same power, a higher voltage needs less current.

electrification.short: Switching a use of energy, such as heating or driving, from burning fuel to using electricity.

electrolyzer.short: A machine that uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

emissions-cap.short: A limit on the total CO2 that may be emitted in a period, such as a year.

energization.short: Switching on a customer's grid service, so that power can flow to it.

energy.short: An amount of electricity made or used over a stretch of time, equal to power multiplied by time and measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) or megawatt-hours (MWh).

energy-burden.short: The share of a household's income spent on energy bills.

energy-carrier.short: A form in which energy is moved to where it is used, such as electricity, natural gas, gasoline or hydrogen.

energy-security.short: Keeping energy flowing at bearable prices when a fuel, a supplier or a route is cut off.

energy-service.short: What people actually want from energy, such as a warm room, hot water, cold food, light or a trip; the energy is only the means.

energy-storage.short: Equipment, such as a battery, that takes in electricity at one time and gives it back later, with some losses.

enrichment.short: Raising the share of uranium-235 in uranium: natural uranium has just over 0.7%, and power-plant fuel in the United States 3% to 5%.

epsg-code.short: A catalogue number that names one coordinate system exactly, such as EPSG:4326 for latitude and longitude in degrees.

epsilon-constraint.short: A way to trace a trade-off by optimizing one goal while capping the other, then moving the cap step by step.

ercot.short: The Electric Reliability Council of Texas: the grid operator, and its wholesale market, for most of Texas.

ethics-board.short: The committee that reviews research with people before it starts; in the United States, an institutional review board.

evidence-ladder.short: The stages a project climbs: announced, funded, permitted, under construction, operating and at design output.

exogenous.short: Set from outside a model as an input, rather than worked out by the model.

expected-unserved-energy.short: Demand left unmet, averaged over many simulated years, in MWh a year: an amount of energy, unlike a load's size in MW.

expected-value.short: The long-run average of an uncertain quantity: each possible outcome multiplied by its chance, then added up.

external-cost.short: A cost that falls on people outside a deal, such as the damage from CO₂, which neither the buyer nor the seller pays.

falsification-statement.short: A sentence naming the result that would show your expected answer wrong.

fast-frequency-response.short: Power from batteries or other inverter-based resources delivered within a fraction of a second of a frequency drop.

feasible-region.short: The set of all plans that meet every rule of a model; on a two-variable chart it is a shaded polygon.

feedback-loop.short: A chain of causes that leads back to where it started, so a change comes back to push on itself.

feeder.short: A distribution line that carries power from a substation to the homes and businesses along it.

fermi-estimate.short: A quick estimate built from round numbers and a few simple steps, aiming to get the order of magnitude right.

final-energy.short: The energy a home, business or vehicle buys and uses, as on its meters and receipts, such as kWh of electricity or gallons of gasoline.

firm-capacity.short: Power that can be counted on whenever it is needed, whatever the weather.

firm-output.short: Power a plant can be counted on to deliver steadily, such as the same output in every hour.

firm-share.short: The part of a plant's capacity that a grid counts on in its riskiest hours, often estimated as its effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) and set per technology class.

fission.short: The splitting of a heavy atom, such as uranium-235, into two smaller atoms when it absorbs a neutron, which releases heat and a few new neutrons.

fixed-charge.short: A part of a power bill that is the same each month however much electricity the home uses.

fixed-om.short: Operation and maintenance costs a plant pays every year whether or not it runs, such as staff and insurance.

flexibility.short: The ability of a plant, a store or a group of users to raise or lower power quickly when the grid asks.

flow.short: A rate that fills or drains a stock, such as megawatts into a battery or tonnes of CO₂ a year; only flows change a stock.

forecast-error.short: The difference between what was forecast, such as tomorrow's demand or wind, and what actually happened.

frozen-telemetry.short: A measurement feed stuck on its last value, which shows up as the same reading hour after hour.

fuel-assembly.short: A bundle of fuel rods, each a sealed metal tube of stacked uranium pellets, loaded into a reactor core as one unit.

fuel-cell.short: A device that turns hydrogen (and oxygen from the air) into electricity, with water as the by-product: an electrolyzer run backwards.

fuse.short: A wire that melts on a fault and cuts the power beyond it; a crew must replace it.

gas-turbine.short: An engine that compresses air, burns fuel in it and lets the hot gas spin a turbine, as a jet engine does; alone it is a simple-cycle plant, such as a peaker.

generator.short: A machine that turns the spin of a shaft into electricity, by turning magnets past coils of wire.

geothermal.short: Electricity made from the earth's heat, using hot water or steam brought up from wells.

gigawatt.short: A thousand megawatts, a rate of energy flow used for large plants, whole fleets and national demand.

gis.short: Software and methods for mapping and analysing data tied to places, such as land use, lines and population.

global-sensitivity-analysis.short: Ranking a model's inputs by their influence on a result while all of them vary together across their assumed ranges, rather than one at a time.

governor.short: A plant's speed control that opens or closes its steam, gas or water valves as the grid frequency changes.

frequency.short: The number of cycles per second of the grid's alternating current, 60 hertz (Hz) in North America, which falls when power is short and rises when there is too much.

grid-following.short: Said of an inverter, such as an ordinary solar inverter, that follows a voltage something else sets and stops when there is none.

grid-forming.short: Said of an inverter or a generator that sets voltage and frequency itself, so it can start and hold an island with no grid behind it.

git-head.short: Git's name for the commit you are on now; usually it points at a branch label, which points at that commit.

hydraulic-head.short: The height the water falls through a hydro plant, from the reservoir's surface down to where it leaves the turbine, in metres.

heat-engine.short: A machine that turns part of a flow of heat into motion, such as a steam or gas turbine; the hotter its heat source, the larger the part it can turn.

heat-pump.short: A device that uses electricity to move heat, into a building to warm it or out of it to cool it.

heat-rate.short: The fuel energy a power plant burns to make one megawatt-hour, for example in MMBtu per MWh, so lower means more efficient.

hrsg.short: The boiler of a combined-cycle plant, heated by the gas turbine's hot exhaust instead of a flame.

hidden-state.short: Values in a notebook's memory that no longer match the code on the page, for example after a cell was edited but not rerun.

high-temperature-electrolyzer.short: An electrolyzer that splits steam at several hundred degrees Celsius; part of the energy comes as heat, so it needs less electricity per kilogram.

histogram.short: A chart that sorts values into bins of equal width and shows how many fall in each bin.

horizon.short: The span of time a study covers, from a day of operation to decades of planning.

hour-ending.short: A time stamp that labels each hour by its last moment, so 01:00 means the hour from midnight to 01:00.

hourly-matching.short: A rule that each hour's electricity use is covered by clean generation in that same hour, rather than over a whole year.

independent-events.short: Events where knowing that one happened says nothing about whether the other did, so the chance of both is the product of their chances.

inequality.short: A rule that allows a range of values, written with ≤ (at most) or ≥ (at least).

inertia.short: Energy stored in the spinning machines of a power grid; it slows a fall in frequency but cannot stop it.

infeasible.short: Said of a model whose rules contradict each other, so that no plan meets them all.

inflation.short: The rise in prices in general over time, so that a dollar buys less each year.

informed-consent.short: A person's agreement to take part in research, given freely after being told what will happen, the risks and how their data will be used.

internal-rate-of-return.short: The discount rate at which a project's net present value is exactly zero: the return the project itself earns.

inverter.short: Power electronics that convert the direct current of solar panels and batteries, or a wind turbine's varying output, into the grid's alternating current.

islanding.short: A microgrid or part of a grid disconnecting from the main grid and keeping its own loads supplied.

kilowatt.short: A unit of power equal to 1,000 watts.

kilowatt-hour.short: The unit of energy on a household electricity bill: one kilowatt kept up for one hour.

large-load-tariff.short: A tariff for very large new customers, such as data centers or factories, with terms that protect other customers if the load uses less than it promised.

lateral.short: A side branch of a distribution feeder that serves one street or block, often protected by its own fuse.

latin-hypercube.short: A way to draw many sets of uncertain inputs so that the whole range of every input is covered evenly.

lcoe.short: A plant's lifetime costs divided by the electricity it makes over its life, both discounted to today's money, giving an average cost per megawatt-hour.

lcoh.short: The cost of making one kilogram of hydrogen over a plant's life: discounted lifetime costs divided by discounted lifetime kilograms (with the same cost and output every year, one year's annualized cost divided by one year's kilograms, as in CF2's toy).

life-cycle-assessment.short: Counting a product's environmental effects, such as CO₂ emissions or water use, over its whole life, from materials to disposal.

linear-program.short: An optimization problem in which the goal and all the rules are linear, so each is a sum of quantities times fixed numbers.

load-factor.short: Average demand over a period divided by the peak demand in that period.

load-relief.short: The small drop in demand when the frequency falls, because many motors turn a little slower and draw less power.

load-duration-curve.short: A year's hourly demand sorted from highest to lowest, showing for how many hours each level of demand is needed.

local-optimum.short: The best plan for one part of a system judged inside its own boundary, which need not be best for the system it sits in.

locational-marginal-price.short: The extra cost per megawatt-hour of serving a small increase in demand at one place on the grid in one interval, given the plants running and the limits of the lines.

log-scale.short: A scale on which each equal step multiplies the value by the same factor, often 10, so tiny and huge values fit on one chart.

logistics-cost.short: The cost of moving and storing goods between factories, warehouses and stores: shipping, warehousing and handling.

long-duration-storage.short: Storage that can give its full power for about 10 hours or more; DOE splits it into inter-day (10 to 36 hours) and multi-day or week-long (36 to 160 hours) stores.

lole.short: The expected number of days a year on which supply falls short of demand at least once, of any size or length, averaged over many simulated years; an expectation, not a count of real outages.

lower-bound.short: A value the best answer cannot fall below; in a cost-minimising model, the cost of a relaxation is one.

lp-relaxation.short: The same model with every whole-number decision allowed to take any value in between, such as a switch anywhere from 0 to 1; its best cost is a lower bound for the real model.

major-event-day.short: A day with so many outage minutes, usually from a big storm, that it passes a threshold set from a utility's past five years (IEEE 1366); reports give reliability with and without them.

margin.short: What a business earns from its output after paying its operating costs: revenue minus operating costs.

marginal-cost.short: What one more unit costs, here the extra running cost of one more megawatt-hour of demand.

marginal-emission-factor.short: The change in a grid's total CO₂ caused by a small change in electricity demand; in Prairie Town, the CO₂ rate of the next plant that responds.

marginal-plant.short: The plant that serves the last megawatt of demand, whose offer sets the clearing price.

matrix.short: A table of numbers in rows and columns; in a model, one row per rule and one column per decision.

mcda.short: Scoring options against several goals at once, such as cost, emissions and fairness, with weights that the people deciding set.

mean.short: The average of a set of values: their sum divided by how many there are.

mae.short: The average size of a forecast's misses, in the units of what is forecast, ignoring whether they were too high or too low.

mape.short: The average miss as a percentage of the actual value; it breaks down when actual values are near zero.

median.short: The middle value of a set sorted from lowest to highest: half the values lie below it, half above.

medoid.short: The member of a group whose total distance to the other members is smallest; unlike an average, it is a real member.

megawatt.short: A unit of power equal to one million watts, or a thousand kilowatts.

megawatt-hour.short: A unit of energy: one megawatt kept up for one hour, or a thousand kilowatt-hours.

merge.short: Joining two lines of commits into one, keeping the changes made on both.

merit-order.short: Running power plants in order of their running cost, cheapest first.

meshed-network.short: A network with loops, so power can reach a place by more than one path, as transmission networks do.

method-family.short: A group of research methods that answer the same kind of question in a similar way, such as optimization, simulation or statistics.

microgrid.short: A local group of loads and sources, such as a campus or a village, that is managed as one system and can disconnect from the main grid and run on its own.

mini-grid.short: A small local grid, with its own sources, storage and wires, that serves a village or a town that the main grid does not reach.

minimum-billing-demand.short: The least demand, often a share of the contracted kW or MW, that a customer is billed for each month however low its demand.

minimum-down-time.short: The hours a plant must stay off once stopped before it may start again.

minimum-load.short: The lowest output at which a machine can keep running; below it the machine must stop, such as an electrolyzer below a set share of its size.

minimum-run-time.short: The hours a plant must stay on once started; the minimum down time is the hours it must stay off once stopped.

minimum-stable-output.short: The lowest output at which a running plant can operate steadily; below it the plant must switch off.

mixed-integer-program.short: An optimization model in which some decisions must be whole numbers, such as a plant being on (1) or off (0).

mmbtu.short: One million British thermal units, a unit of fuel heat; about 0.29 MWh of heat, and gas is priced in dollars per MMBtu.

moderator.short: A material, such as ordinary water or graphite, that slows the fast neutrons from fission so that uranium-235 captures them more easily.

monte-carlo.short: A method that runs a calculation many times on randomly drawn inputs and reads the spread of the results.

monte-carlo-error.short: How far an estimate from a Monte Carlo study would move with another random seed; it shrinks roughly with the square root of the number of runs.

multi-objective.short: A choice with several goals that cannot all be at their best at once.

multiplication-factor.short: In a chain reaction, the number of new fissions each fission leads to on average: below 1 the chain dies out, at 1 it holds steady, above 1 it grows.

mw-it.short: Megawatts of a data center's computing equipment; the grid must supply more, for cooling and the rest of the building.

mwt-mwe.short: Megawatts of heat (thermal) and megawatts of electricity (electric); a plant's MWe is its MWt times its efficiency.

nadir.short: The lowest point the frequency reaches after a power plant trips, before it starts to recover.

negative-price.short: A wholesale price below zero, which happens when the last plant needed would rather pay than stop running.

net-billing.short: A billing rule under which kWh sent back to the grid earn a credit set separately from the retail price, often the value of energy in that hour.

net-demand.short: Demand minus the output of wind and solar, which is what the other power plants must still supply.

net-metering.short: A billing rule under which each kWh a customer sends back to the grid earns the same price as a kWh it buys.

net-present-value.short: The present value of a project's future income minus the present value of its costs; above zero, it earns more than it costs at the chosen discount rate.

net-zero.short: The point at which the CO₂ a country or the world adds to the air each year is balanced by the CO₂ it removes, so that cumulative emissions stop rising.

net-benefit-test.short: A check that an option's total benefits across all affected parties exceed its total costs, each counted once.

neutron.short: A particle with no electric charge in the nucleus of an atom; in a reactor, the neutrons from one fission go on to split more atoms.

no-load-cost.short: What a plant costs for each hour it is on, before it makes any power.

nominal-rate.short: An interest or discount rate that includes inflation, used with cash counted in the dollars of each future year.

normal-distribution.short: A symmetric, bell-shaped spread of values set by its mean and standard deviation, also called Gaussian; about 68% of its values lie within one standard deviation of the mean.

notebook.short: A document of code cells and text, such as a Jupyter notebook: you run each cell on its own, and its output appears under it.

notebook-kernel.short: The running program behind a notebook that holds its variables in memory between cells, whatever order the cells were run in.

n-minus-one.short: A planning rule: the system keeps serving its customers after any one element, such as a line, fails.

objective.short: What an optimization tries to make as small or as large as possible, such as the total cost.

operating-emissions.short: The CO2 released where fuel is burned to make electricity, leaving out building the plant and producing and delivering its fuel.

optimality-gap.short: For a mixed-integer program, the remaining distance between the best plan the solver has found and the bound it has proven, so 0% means proven best.

optimization.short: Finding the best choice among many, given a goal and the rules the choice must obey.

optimization-window.short: The stretch of time, such as a month, within which a model may move electricity use between hours while keeping the total over that stretch.

order-of-magnitude.short: The power of ten a quantity sits at; two quantities are an order of magnitude apart when one is about ten times the other.

outlet-temperature.short: The temperature of the coolant as it leaves a reactor core; it sets how hot the heat is that a plant can supply.

overnight-cost.short: The cost to build a power plant as if it were built overnight, so with no interest paid during construction, usually given per kilowatt.

parameter.short: A number a model is given and takes as it is, such as demand or a plant's running cost, as opposed to a decision it makes.

pareto-frontier.short: The set of plans that cannot be made cheaper without becoming dirtier, or cleaner without becoming more expensive.

passive-safety.short: Safety features that rely on natural effects, such as hot fluid rising and cool fluid sinking, instead of pumps, outside power or operators.

payback-period.short: The number of years until the running sum of a project's cash first gets back to zero, with or without discounting.

peak-demand.short: The highest demand in a period, such as the busiest hour of a year; the grid must be able to meet it, with a margin.

peaker.short: A power plant that runs only in the hours of highest demand, because it starts quickly but is expensive to run.

penalty.short: An extra cost added to a model's objective for an action it should not take too freely, such as adjusting an hour's load.

penstock.short: The large pipe that carries water down from a reservoir to a hydro plant's turbine.

percentile.short: The value that a given share of a sorted set stays at or below: 90% of values are at or below the 90th percentile.

perfect-foresight.short: A model assumption that every future value in the horizon, such as tomorrow's demand and weather, is known when decisions are made; it gives an upper bound on what flexibility can earn.

period-weight.short: How many hours of the year one modelled hour of a representative period stands for; a model multiplies that hour's running cost and emissions by it.

persistence-forecast.short: The simplest forecast: the next value will be the same as the last one seen, or as the same hour a day or a week before.

photovoltaic.short: Solar panels that turn sunlight directly into electricity.

point-of-common-coupling.short: The one place where a microgrid meets the main grid, with the switch that opens to let it run on its own.

power.short: How fast electricity is being made or used at a given moment, measured in watts, kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW).

power-coefficient.short: The share of the wind's power that a turbine turns into electricity; no rotor can capture more than 16/27, about 59% (the Betz limit).

power-curve.short: A chart of how much power a wind turbine makes at each wind speed.

power-purchase-agreement.short: A long contract between a power plant's seller and a buyer that sets the price paid for the plant's power, or for its market value.

prediction-interval.short: A range that should contain the actual value with a stated probability, drawn as a band around a forecast.

present-value.short: What an amount of money paid or received in the future is worth today, once it is discounted.

pricing-node.short: A point on the grid, such as a power plant's connection, where the market sets its own price.

primary-energy.short: Energy as found in nature before any conversion, such as the gas burned in a power plant to make the electricity a home later buys.

primary-response.short: Automatic extra output from power plants' governors within seconds of a frequency drop; it stops the fall but does not restore 60 Hz.

probability-distribution.short: A rule that says how likely each value of an uncertain input is; a uniform distribution makes every value in its range equally likely.

procurement-rule.short: A rule for which purchased electricity a buyer may count as clean, for example by region, by hour and by how new the plant is; it sets a claim, not the emissions the purchase causes.

production-credit.short: A payment for each megawatt-hour a plant produces, set by a policy such as a tax credit.

productive-use.short: Electricity used to earn a living, such as running a grain mill, a water pump or a cold store, rather than only for lights and phones at home.

prognostics.short: Predicting when a machine part is likely to fail, from data on its condition, so that repairs can be planned before it does.

projection.short: A model's estimate of a future quantity under stated assumptions, not a measurement or a promise.

provenance.short: The documented origin and history of a piece of data: source, version, access date, checksums and every change made to it.

quartile.short: The values that cut a sorted set into four equal parts: 25% of values lie below the first, 50% below the second (the median), 75% below the third.

question-type.short: The kind of answer a research question asks for: descriptive, explanatory, evaluative, predictive or prescriptive.

radial-network.short: A network shaped like a tree, with one path from the source to each customer, as most distribution feeders are.

ramp-rate.short: How fast a power plant can raise or lower its output, for example in megawatts per minute or per hour.

random-seed.short: A fixed starting number for a random-number generator, so a random draw comes out the same on every run.

rank-correlation.short: The correlation of the ranks of two quantities, from −1 to 1: how consistently one rises or falls with the other, whatever the shape of the link.

rocof.short: How fast the grid's frequency moves in the first instant after a disturbance, in hertz per second.

rated-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine first reaches its full rated power; above it, the blades turn to spill the extra wind.

ratepayer.short: A customer who pays a utility's regulated electricity rates; utility costs that nobody else covers end up in those rates.

reactance.short: A line's opposition to alternating current; when several paths join two places, each carries a share of the power that falls as its reactance rises.

reactive-power.short: The part of alternating-current power that does no net work but holds voltage up; it is supplied and absorbed locally.

real-rate.short: An interest or discount rate with inflation taken out, used with costs stated in one year's dollars.

real-time-pricing.short: A tariff whose price per kWh follows the wholesale or system price hour by hour, so the bill moves with it.

rebound-effect.short: Part of an efficiency saving taken back because the cheaper service gets used more.

recloser.short: A breaker on a feeder that opens on a fault and tries closing again in seconds, so a passing fault, such as a brushing branch, causes only a blink.

refuelling-outage.short: The planned weeks when a reactor is shut down to replace part of its fuel and carry out maintenance.

reinforcing-loop.short: A feedback loop with an even number of negative links, in which a change feeds itself, as growth or as decline.

relative-growth-index.short: How fast a topic's paper count grew from 2016–18 to 2022–24, divided by the growth of energy-systems research as a whole.

repository.short: A project folder together with its full history of commits, as kept by a version-control tool such as Git.

representative-period.short: A real stretch of time, such as a week, chosen to stand for many similar ones so that a model can run faster.

resample.short: Regroup a time series to a coarser step, such as hours to days, by averaging or summing.

research-gap.short: A question the literature has not answered, shown with a logged search and the closest prior work, not just asserted.

reserve-margin.short: The capacity counted as available at the peak, above the year's peak demand, as a percentage of that peak.

reserves.short: Spare capacity that operators keep ready to cover the sudden loss of a plant or a forecast that misses.

reservoir.short: The lake a dam holds back; its water is energy stored for later, up to what it holds.

reservoir-limit.short: The lowest and highest level a store may hold, such as a tank's minimum pressure or a reservoir's lowest water level; a model writes it as bounds on the level.

resource-adequacy.short: Whether a power system has enough supply to meet demand in nearly every hour, judged with many weather years and plant outages against a criterion such as a loss-of-load expectation.

rolling-horizon.short: Planning over a window ahead on a forecast, carrying out only the first hours of the plan, then planning again as the real values arrive.

round-trip-efficiency.short: The share of the energy put into storage that comes back out.

run-of-river.short: A hydro plant with little or no reservoir, so it makes what the river's flow brings at the time.

running-cost.short: What it costs a plant to make one more megawatt-hour, mostly fuel, leaving out the cost of building it.

saidi.short: System Average Interruption Duration Index: the minutes without power the average customer has in a year, customer-minutes divided by customers served.

saifi.short: System Average Interruption Frequency Index: the number of interruptions the average customer has in a year, customers interrupted divided by customers served.

system-scale.short: A level of an energy system, from one device or plant to a whole nation, set apart by who decides what and by the physics a model of it needs.

scarcity-price.short: A very high wholesale price in hours when available supply barely covers demand.

scenario.short: A coherent what-if set of a model's inputs, such as a 36-month wait; a scenario may be given a probability, though this lesson gives none.

scientific-notation.short: A way to write a number as a value at least 1 and less than 10, times a power of ten, so very large and very small numbers are easy to compare.

search-string.short: The words and operators (AND, OR, quotation marks) typed into a literature database to find papers.

sector-coupling.short: Linking energy carriers such as electricity, hydrogen and heat through devices that convert one into another, so that one carrier's supply and price affect the others.

sensitivity-analysis.short: Changing a model's inputs one at a time and re-solving, to see which inputs the answer depends on.

service-level.short: The share of cases in which a rule must hold, such as meeting store demand in 95 of every 100 weeks.

shadow-price.short: How much the best total cost would change if one rule were loosened by one unit; for the rule that supply equals demand, it is the price of one more megawatt-hour.

simplex-method.short: A way to solve linear programs by moving from corner to neighbouring corner of the feasible region, never making the goal worse, until no neighbour is better.

skill-score.short: How much smaller a forecast's error is than that of a simple baseline such as persistence.

snowballing.short: Finding papers from one you already have: backward through its references, forward through the works that cite it.

solver.short: Software that finds the best solution of an optimization problem, or shows that none exists.

spent-fuel.short: Fuel that has been used in a reactor and taken out; it is solid, highly radioactive and still warm, and is kept first in water pools, later in dry casks.

staged-energization.short: Switching on part of a large load's grid service early and the rest later, as the grid becomes ready.

staging-area.short: Git's list of changes picked for the next commit: git add puts a file's current version there.

stakeholder.short: A person or group affected by a study or the decision it informs, or able to affect it.

standard-deviation.short: A measure of spread: roughly, how far a typical value lies from the mean.

standard-error.short: How far an estimate from a random sample typically lands from the value for the whole set; it shrinks as the sample grows.

standing-loss.short: Energy a store loses while it waits, used or not, such as heat leaking from a hot tank; it grows with time, unlike the loss of each charge and discharge.

start-up-cost.short: The fuel and wear spent to bring a plant from off to on, paid once per start.

start-up-time.short: How long a plant takes to go from shut down to full output; the ramp rate is how fast it changes output once running.

state-of-charge.short: The energy a battery holds at a given moment, in MWh; it links each hour of a storage schedule to the next.

steam-generator.short: A heat exchanger in which hot water from a reactor's sealed loop boils the water of a second, separate loop into steam.

steam-turbine.short: A turbine spun by high-pressure steam from a boiler or another heat source.

stock.short: An amount that builds up or drains over time, such as water in a reservoir, energy in a battery or CO₂ emitted so far.

stranded-cost.short: Money already spent on equipment that is no longer used as planned, such as grid upgrades built for a load that never arrives.

stylized-network.short: A simplified, made-up network built to show how a model behaves, with invented distances and costs rather than a real company's map.

substation.short: A fenced yard of transformers, breakers and switches where the grid changes voltage and where feeders start.

supply-diversity.short: How evenly the energy supply is spread over different sources, so that losing one does not lose most of it.

supply-stack.short: All the offers to sell power in one hour, lined up from the cheapest to the most expensive.

synchronous-grid.short: A grid whose generators all turn in step at one shared frequency; the Lower 48 states have three main ones, called interconnections.

synthetic-sample.short: A few invented records with the same columns and realistic values as data that cannot be shared, so others can run the code without the real data.

system-boundary.short: The line that decides which parts, costs and emissions a study counts and which it leaves out.

tariff.short: The rule for calculating electricity bills: fixed charges, prices per kWh, or both.

techno-economic-analysis.short: Estimating what a technology costs and earns from its engineering design, its prices and its operating pattern.

techno-economic-optimization.short: A model that compares equipment sizes and ways of running them by both their performance and their cost, and picks the best for a stated goal.

telemetry.short: Measurements sent automatically from plants and substations to the grid operator.

terawatt-hour.short: A unit of energy equal to a billion kilowatt-hours, used for the yearly electricity use of regions and countries.

thermal-storage.short: Storing energy as heat, for example in tanks of hot molten salt, to use it hours later.

time-step.short: The length of one step in a model or dataset, such as five minutes, an hour or a year.

time-of-use.short: A retail electricity price that changes with the hour of the day, higher at peak times and lower off-peak.

time-of-use-tariff.short: An electricity price that changes with the hour of the day, usually higher in the evening peak.

time-series-aggregation.short: Shrinking a long series, such as a year of hours, to a few representative periods that a model can solve quickly.

tolling-agreement.short: A contract in which the buyer pays the owner of a plant a fixed fee for the right to run it, and keeps what it earns.

tornado-chart.short: A chart that ranks inputs by how far a result moves when each input is swung from a low to a high value, one at a time.

tracked-file.short: A file Git already knows, because it is in the last commit or the staging area; a new file stays untracked until git add.

trading-hub.short: A pricing point where many contracts are settled, priced as an average over many nodes of the grid.

transactive-energy.short: Buying and selling electricity among many small participants, such as homes and firms with their own generation, as well as with the grid.

transformer.short: A device with two coils that raises or lowers an alternating voltage, such as from 18 kV to 345 kV at a plant or from 12.47 kV to 240/120 V near a home.

transmission.short: The high-voltage part of the grid (115 to 765 kV in the U.S.) that carries power over long distances between plants, regions and substations.

turbine.short: A machine whose blades are pushed round by moving gas, steam, water or wind, turning a shaft.

unbounded.short: Said of a model whose goal can improve without limit, which usually means a rule is missing.

ufls.short: Relays that automatically disconnect blocks of customers when the frequency falls to a set level, to save the rest of the grid.

unit-commitment.short: Deciding which plants are on in each hour, before deciding how much each one produces.

unserved-energy.short: Demand that could not be met, so some customers lost power.

uplift.short: A payment outside the market price that covers costs a scheduled plant cannot recover at the price, such as start-up and no-load costs; also called a make-whole payment.

useful-energy.short: The part of the energy bought that a device actually delivers as the wanted heat, light or motion, after its own losses.

utm.short: A set of 60 north-to-south zones, each a flat map in metres that keeps distances close to true inside the zone.

validation.short: Checking that a model represents the real system well enough for the question it is used to answer.

value-of-coupling.short: How much cheaper a system is with devices that link its carriers than with each carrier supplied on its own, judged as a difference of optimal costs.

value-of-lost-load.short: What a customer loses when power is cut, per hour or per kWh not delivered; it differs by customer and by how long the outage lasts.

variable-om.short: Operation and maintenance costs, apart from fuel, that grow with every megawatt-hour a plant makes.

variable-renewables.short: Wind and solar power, whose output follows the weather: they can be turned down but not up.

vector.short: An ordered list of numbers, such as a plan's outputs, in which the position of each number carries its meaning.

verification.short: Checking that a model does what its equations say, with tests such as units, the energy balance and hand-solved cases.

version-control.short: Keeping every saved state of a project's files, with who changed what and why, so any earlier state can be compared or brought back.

virtual-power-plant.short: Many small devices, such as batteries, thermostats and chargers, controlled together and offered to the grid as one resource.

voltage.short: The electrical push that drives current through a wire, measured in volts (V); 1 kilovolt (kV) is 1,000 V.

waste-heat.short: Heat a power plant cannot turn into electricity and releases to the air or to cooling water.

watt-hour.short: A unit of energy: one watt kept up for one hour; 1,000 Wh make one kilowatt-hour.

web-mercator.short: The projection most web maps use: good for viewing, but it stretches distances and areas more the farther a place is from the equator.

wacc.short: The blended return a project must pay its lenders and its owners, used as the project's discount rate.

weighted-sum.short: A way to combine several goals into one score by adding them up, each multiplied by a weight.

wholesale-price.short: The price at which electricity is traded between power plants and the companies that sell it to customers, often set hour by hour.
